title: Jane Lynch Wants to Return for ‘Glee’ Reboot: ‘I Would Love to Do Sue Sylvester for the Rest of My Life’
description: Sue Sylvester may soon be terrorizing the students of William McKinley High School once again — that is, if Jane Lynch has anything to do with it.
body:
Sue Sylvester may soon be terrorizing the students of William McKinley High School once again — that is, if Jane Lynch has anything to do with it. 

	After the “Glee” reboot was officially greenlit last month at Disney+ and Hulu, speculation started swirling about who from the original cast might return. During an appearance on “The Jennifer Hudson Show” on Monday, Lynch made it clear that she’d be happy to reprise her role as the foul-mouthed cheer coach.
	

	“If I am asked to partake, the answer will be yes,” Lynch told Hudson. “I cannot wait.” 

	Asked what it would be like to revisit the character, Lynch said: “Oh, I would love to do Sue Sylvester for the rest of my life. You know, I wonder though how far we can take her now. Because if you look out in the world, there are a lot of Sue Sylvesters out there.”

	Indeed, the Emmy winner previously said in a 2022 interview with The Guardian that Sylvester “would be MAGA” if “Glee” ever came back. She added that if the show were airing today, “I think there would have been people out there who would have wanted to cancel Sue Sylvester.” 

	However, she told Hudson that “it would be really, really fun to do it again and to get to wear tracksuits every day. That was my most favorite wardrobe.”

	As for the rest of the original cast, Variety has confirmed that Lea Michele will be returning as Glee Club leader Rachel Berry. Several other original stars have also expressed their interest in taking part in the reboot, including Kurt Hummel actor Chris Colfer, who told The Daily Beast’s “Obsessed” podcast last week that conversations about his return are ongoing. 
	

	“From what I heard, it sounded very funny and it sounded like a good idea. So we’ll see,” Colfer said, even pitching some potential Kurt storylines: “I would love to see him like a Miranda Priestly-type, running his own fashion blog or a magazine. I could also see him on tour with Chappell Roan, styling her. There’s a lot of fun avenues they could explore.”

	Watch Lynch’s full interview with Hudson below.

schema.headline: Jane Lynch Wants to Return for ‘Glee’ Reboot: ‘I Would Love to Do Sue Sylvester for the Rest of My Life’

title: Schiwago Film Boards ‘Southwest,’ With Avi Nash and Antoine Reinartz, and ‘Anatol,’ Readies Tallinn Bow of ‘The Matriarch’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
German production company Schiwago has boarded adventure film “Southwest” by Ika Künzel and Wolfgang Fischer. The duo is also behind “Styx.” 

	Set
body:
German production company Schiwago has boarded adventure film “Southwest” by Ika Künzel and Wolfgang Fischer. The duo is also behind “Styx.” 

	Set to be shoot in Namibia, it will star Avi Nash (“Silo,” “The Walking Dead”) and Antoine Reinartz (“Anatomy of a Fall,” “120 BPM”).

	Schiwago Film will also produce “Anatol” by Lukas Nathrath, his second feature after “One Last Evening,” and Lisa Charlotte Friederich’s “The Good German.”
	

	“We have a pretty exciting year ahead of us,” said producer Philipp Goeser.

	“It’s a wide array of topics and styles, but at the core are handpicked stories that are very authentic and personal. We’re always looking for authentic new voices and stories. Most of our [upcoming] titles are debut films, which is a very important focus for the company.”

	This includes elevated thriller “The Matriarch,” which will have its world premiere at the 30th Black Nights Film Festival. Sold by Pluto Film, it’ll be distributed in Germany by Four Guys Film Distribution.

	The film follows 17-year-old Kim, who enters her mother’s trafficking business. They bring Vietnamese migrants to Europe and, predictably, others want a piece of the pie as well.

	“We work very closely with the artists. We want to support their vision and ‘The Matriarch’ is a perfect example of that,” said Goeser.

	It’s the first film with an almost exclusively Vietnamese-German cast, one that features Tuyen Do, Viet Pham, Trang Le Hong, Lissy-Marie Nguyen, Viet Long Hoang and Marlon Minh-Hai Leyck. Its director, Alison Kuhn, is Vietnamese-German as well.
	

	“Our projects are arthouse, but they also have a commercial side. Alison and I discussed that very early on. How can we tell an edgy family drama about a mother and a daughter and also give it a genre twist?”

	Kuhn agreed: “Personally, I wish arthouse and mainstream cinema would find their way back to each other rather than drifting further and further apart. As someone who directs both commercial streaming series and auteur-driven, personal films, I’d love for us to rediscover the magical sweet spot that existed in cinema before the turn of the millennium.”

	Growing up as a biracial German-Vietnamese child, she only saw people on screen who resembled one half of her family.

	“Having had the privilege of studying directing at a prestigious film school, I wanted to use my position behind the camera to create complex, breathing protagonists of Vietnamese descent who aren’t the nerdy overachiever providing comic relief or the waitress who appears in just one scene, speaking with a stereotypical accent,” she said.

	Kuhn wanted to bring a different perspective to the table and to look at her protagonists with empathy.

	“To me, empathy is probably the most important word in filmmaking. I want to understand what drives my main characters to make certain choices, even when those choices might be morally questionable,” she noted.

	“Although the film is told from the daughter’s perspective, it was important to understand the mother as well. As a woman in the diaspora who has never been accepted as an equal by German society, she has achieved an incredible amount through sheer determination. She has built a system that provides stability for her family in Vietnam and her children in Germany, but it comes at an enormous cost to her.”

	In the film, the mother wants to protect her daughter from that life but ultimately has to accept her help.

	“The daughter, Kim, is our emotional anchor throughout the story. She experiences things that anyone who has ever been a teenager can relate to: curiosity about the world, the discovery of romance and sexuality, the desire to experiment and find her own identity.”

	In a way, though, Kim can also be seen as a reflection of her mother’s younger self, forced to sacrifice her personal desires.
	

	“My hope is that audiences will feel the love between mother and daughter and root for them to find their way to each other.”

	“The Matriarch” is produced by Martin Lehwald, Goeser and Marcos Kantis, while Paula Elina Klossner and Stephan Buske co-produce.

	“Anatol,” sold by Beta Cinema, will be a lighter proposition. It shows a boy who, after studying philosophy, finds himself on a job-hunting odyssey full of quirky encounters, family rivalries, white lies and mishaps.

	“It’s a tragicomedy with an arthouse story,” said Goeser, comparing the film to the works of Joachim Trier. “The script is amazing and it’s really, really funny.”

	Filming will begin in January, with Alamode set to distribute in Germany.

	“The Good German” is a historical drama about Duala Manga Bell, the German-educated Cameroonian king who fought the colonial seizure of Duala land through the courts. He was executed after a sham trial in 1914.

	Beside him – yet ultimately against him – is Hermann Röhm, a childhood acquaintance turned colonial official.

	Other new projects include “Ruki’s First Summer” and TV series “Nuclear Sunset Cruise,” both inspired by true events yet completely different.

	“Ruki’s First Summer” will be Schiwago Film’s first children’s and family film. Directed by Frédérique Veith, it’s written by Zazou Röver and features Bellamine Abdelmalek (“I Lost My Body”).

	In the story, a disastrous summer vacation strands 10-year-old Sarah and an old soup chicken in the vast Tunisian desert, launching the greatest adventure of her life, and drawing her closer to both her estranged father and her roots.

	“It’s a sweet tale of growing up between two worlds. It’s a very European topic. Amidst all the negativity surrounding migration, we wanted to demonstrate how children can sometimes solve problems that we, as a society, have been unable to,” noted Goeser.

	“Nuclear Sunset Cruise,” overseen by writer-director Florian Gallenberger and set at the height of the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962, focuses on an East German cruise ship that sails unknowingly into the U.S. naval blockade while en route to Havana.

	“We decided to make it a comedy, and it ended up being like ‘The White Lotus.’ These characters are basically partying while sailing into catastrophe, which I think people might find relatable,” he joked.
	

	“We’re always looking for a unique angle on something important to us. We’ve noticed that people are looking for escapist or lighter stories. However, we also see that as a challenge to give them something that has a deeper layer to it.”

schema.headline: Schiwago Film Boards ‘Southwest,’ With Avi Nash and Antoine Reinartz, and ‘Anatol,’ Readies Tallinn Bow of ‘The Matriarch’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Conquers U.K., Ireland Box Office as ‘Ramayana’ Stays in Top Three
description: Paramount’s gothic reimagining “Ebenezer,” directed by Ti West and starring Johnny Depp as Ebenezer Scrooge alongside Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseboro
body:
Paramount’s gothic reimagining “Ebenezer,” directed by Ti West and starring Johnny Depp as Ebenezer Scrooge alongside Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, and Ian McKellen, debuted at the summit of the U.K. and Ireland box office, collecting £3.9 million ($5.2 million).

	Entertainment Film Distributors’ biographical drama “I Play Rocky,” directed by Peter Farrelly and starring Anthony Ippolito, climbed to second position in its sophomore frame, adding $1.5 million to lift its gross to $3 million. Sony’s Bollywood blockbuster “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” which made history by debuting at No. 1 last week, placed third in its second session with $1.4 million, advancing its total to $5.4 million.
	

	Disney’s “Wild Horse Nine” took fourth spot in its second weekend, collecting $893,441 to raise its cumulative total to $3.8 million. Black Bear’s period comedy “Wicker,” directed by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson and starring Olivia Colman, rounded out the top five in its third frame, adding $865,871 to push its cume to $7.7 million.

	Anime Ltd.’s rollout of “Godzilla Minus Zero” secured sixth position in its second frame, generating $655,147 for a running total of $3.2 million. A24’s dark comedy “Primetime,” directed by Lance Oppenheim and starring Robert Pattinson, placed seventh in its third weekend, taking $594,862 to bring its gross to $5.8 million.

	Lionsgate U.K.’s horror comedy “Ghosts: The Possession of Button House” followed in eighth place in its fourth session, adding $523,796 to advance its cume to $11.2 million. Warner Bros.’ DC horror thriller “Clayface” took ninth position in its fourth frame, generating $450,508 to lift its total haul to $8.9 million. Altitude Film Distribution’s Cannes-winning “La Bola Negra,” directed by Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo and starring Penélope Cruz and Glenn Close, rounded out the top 10 in its second weekend with $384,837, pushing its running cume to $1.4 million.
	

	Just outside the top 10, Sony’s crime comedy “How To Rob A Bank” debuted in 11th spot with $354,774. Universal’s concert film “George Michael: The Faith Tour” placed 12th in its second frame with $332,005 for a $2.2 million cume. Trafalgar Releasing’s event presentation “Festive Fun With Peppa” bowed in 13th place with $327,262. Black Bear’s stop-motion animated fantasy “Wildwood” landed in 14th position in its fourth session, adding $317,997 to reach $5.3 million, while Universal’s animated holdover “Forgotten Island” took 15th spot in its fifth week with $306,658, lifting its total to $7.7 million.

	Further down the chart, Mubi’s sCannes winner “Fatherland,” directed by Paweł Pawlikowski and starring Sandra Hüller, ranked at No. 28 in its fourth weekend – its widest footprint yet across 101 select locations. The title collected $37,802, lifting its cumulative total to $1 million on the heels of winning the Golden Frog at Camerimage and leading the European Film Awards with 11 nominations.

	Looking ahead to the upcoming theatrical frame, mid-week event cinema programming begins on Thursday with Trafalgar Releasing presenting the stage broadcast of “Giant – The Play”.

	Wide commercial and saturation rollouts arriving on Friday across 300+ locations are led by Lionsgate’s tentpole “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” directed by Francis Lawrence and starring Joseph Zada, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, and Elle Fanning; Universal’s thriller “A Talent For Murder,” directed by Anton Corbijn and starring Helen Mirren, Alden Ehrenreich, Olivia Cooke, and Juliet Stevenson; and A24’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.

	Other releases opening Friday include Amazon MGM Studios’ action drama “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” directed by Bassam Tariq and starring Mahershala Ali, John Cho, and Giancarlo Esposito; Disney’s 1986 World Cup sports documentary “The Match,” directed by Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco; Curzon’s Sundance Grand Jury Prize winner “Josephine,” directed by Beth de Araújo and starring Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan; and Netflix’s animated fairy-tale musical “Steps,” directed by Alyce Tzue and John Ripa and featuring the voices of Ali Wong, Amanda Seyfried, Stephanie Hsu, and Bette Midler.
	

	Specialized, festival, and international titles debuting Friday include Icon Film Distribution’s stadium disaster drama “Heysel 85,” directed by Teodora Ana Mihai across 25+ locations; BFI Distribution’s “Filipinana,” directed by Rafael Manuel across 25+ sites; Conic’s Sundance documentary “American Doctor,” directed by Poh Si Teng across 25+ screens; Zee Studios International’s dual Indian releases “70 Syaal” and “Sathyavan Savithri”; and Vue Lumière’s family event “CBeebies Panto 2026: Treasure Island.” Repertory screenings feature Park Circus re-issuing the 15th anniversary edition of Sarah Smith’s animated holiday title “Arthur Christmas,” starring James McAvoy, Hugh Laurie, and Bill Nighy.

	The weekend continues on Saturday with Trafalgar Releasing’s live concert broadcast of “BTS World Tour ‘Arirang’ in Kaohsiung: Live Viewing”, followed on Monday by CinemaLive’s archival screening of “Doctor Who: The Satan Pit.”

schema.headline: Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Conquers U.K., Ireland Box Office as ‘Ramayana’ Stays in Top Three

title: Brad Pitt Pitches Himself to Be Robert Pattinson’s Bond Villain: ‘Sign Me Up’
description: Now that Robert Pattinson has been revealed as the next James Bond, all eyes are on who will be cast as 007’s arch nemesis — and Brad Pitt is putti
body:
Now that Robert Pattinson has been revealed as the next James Bond, all eyes are on who will be cast as 007’s arch nemesis — and Brad Pitt is putting himself up for the job.

	At the premiere of his new film “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” on Monday night, the Oscar winner reacted in real time to the big Bond news, which he hadn’t heard yet. 

	“Is that right?! You know what, I love this idea,” Pitt told Extra TV on the red carpet. “I love what he’s been doing. I love his choices, I think he’s the real deal. That’s great, good call.” 
	

	The new Bond film will be directed by “Dune” helmer Denis Villeneuve for Amazon MGM Studios, which took over creative control of the franchise from longtime producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli last year. 

	Pitt was then asked if he’d be up for the villain role and responded by saying, “Robert! Denis!” with an exaggerated wink to the camera. “You know, I’d like to do that,” he continued. “I’d be up for that. I mean, my man Javier [Bardem] did it so well. It’s tall shoes, but I’d take that on.” 

	Bardem was a Bond baddie in the 2012 film “Skyfall” alongside Daniel Craig. Other actors to take on the task of antagonizing the spy throughout the years include Christopher Walken, Jonathan Pryce, Mads Mikkelsen, Christoph Waltz and Rami Malek. 

	Asked the same question by Complex later on in the night, Pitt was more direct, saying: “Sign me up for the villain. Get Denis Villeneuve on the flip phone, let’s go!” 

	It wouldn’t be the first time Pitt has played a bad guy — he portrayed a serial killer in “Kalifornia,” earned an Oscar nomination as a psychotic mental patient in “12 Monkeys” and “Fight Club’s” Tyler Durden wasn’t exactly a hero. However, all of those roles were in the ’90s towards the beginning of his career, so seeing him embody a villain at this stage could make for a thrilling move.

schema.headline: Brad Pitt Pitches Himself to Be Robert Pattinson’s Bond Villain: ‘Sign Me Up’

title: Disney+ and Hulu App Merger Slated to Be Complete in December
description: Disney‘s years-long effort to unify the Disney+ and Hulu apps is “nearly complete,” Mouse House execs said, as the company looks to concentrate its
body:
Disney‘s years-long effort to unify the Disney+ and Hulu apps is “nearly complete,” Mouse House execs said, as the company looks to concentrate its streaming firepower on the Disney+ platform.

	The company made the announcement in reporting earnings for the September 2026 quarter.

	Beginning this December, Disney+ and Hulu bundle subscribers “will have a fully unified experience on Disney+, including live TV and select premium add-ons, creating a more seamless way to discover and engage with the breadth of content across our brands and franchises,” CEO Josh D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston said in their quarterly letter to shareholders. “We believe our continued focus on product and technology will yield further benefits in engagement and churn over time.”
	

	Also in December, Disney expects to begin introducing creator content on Disney+ through its recent agreement with TikTok. The TikTok content rollout will be “strategically aligned” to the lead-up to Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday” theatrical premiere on Dec. 18, according to the Disney execs. 

	“We are also adding more vertical video, live sports and podcasts to the [Disney+] platform, while continuing to explore other emerging content genres,” D’Amaro and Johnston said.

	Disney’s integration of Hulu and Disney+ kicked off in 2023 under then-CEO Bob Iger, two years before the company closed its deal with Comcast to buy out NBCUniversal‘s one-third stake in Hulu in June 2025.

	Disney has not announced a sunset date for the Hulu app, and as of now Hulu stand-alone subscriptions in the U.S. continue to be available.
	

	This September, Disney announced another round of streaming price hikes, its fourth rate increases in as many years. The pricing strategy is aimed at pushing consumers toward bundles: The Disney+/Hulu Premium bundle increased two dollars, from $19.99 to $21.99/month, which is nearly half what it costs if you purchase them separately, while the ad-supported Disney+/Hulu bundle remained unchanged at $12.99/month (just 50 cents more than each of the services purchased individually).

	According to Disney’s D’Amaro and Johnston, ESPN “plays an important role in the overall Disney portfolio by contributing live and on-demand offerings to Disney+, lifting engagement and supporting revenue growth, and encouraging users to upgrade to the Disney+, Hulu, ESPN bundle.” 

	This fall, Disney increased the volume of sports content we offer Disney+ subscribers without the need for an ESPN subscription. That has included the simulcast of “College GameDay” on Disney+ and adding more live college football games and select NFL games, which kicked off with Dallas Cowboys vs. Philadelphia Eagles on Oct. 26. Following the expansion of ESPN content into Europe and select Asia-Pacific markets this year, ESPN now reaches consumers through Disney+ in about 100 markets.

schema.headline: Disney+ and Hulu App Merger Slated to Be Complete in December

title: Emile Hirsch to Star in Texas-Set Thriller ‘The Violet Crown’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Emile Hirsch is to star in the Texas-set thriller “The Violet Crown,” which begins production in Mississippi and Texas in January.

	Aaron Harvey (
body:
Emile Hirsch is to star in the Texas-set thriller “The Violet Crown,” which begins production in Mississippi and Texas in January.

	Aaron Harvey (“The Neighbor,” “Into The Ashes”) directs from an original screenplay penned by Mark Freiburger (“Between Borders”). Harvey’s latest film, “Come With Me,” starring Theo Rossi and Ron Perlman, premiered to solid reviews in September.

	“The Violet Crown” will see Hirsch play Will Tolbert, a struggling repo man who unknowingly repossesses a crooked cop’s truck and ends up with a duffel bag of stolen cartel cash. According to the filmmakers, it  will evokes the “style of Golden Era ‘70s crime films, like ‘The Conversation.'”
	

	Demetrius Stear (“Bruton,” “Come With Me”) produces via A Mind’s Eye alongside Brinton Bryan (“The Blazing World,” “12 Mighty Orphans”) through his Greenbelt Films banner, and Harvey for Michael Bruce Pictures. 

	“The Violet Crown is an incredible opportunity to showcase Emile’s talents as an actor and put him in the driver seat of an incredibly fast paced, anxiety inducing thriller with a touching, human element,” said Harvey. “I couldn’t be more excited to make this film with him and showcase a side of him that’s yet to be seen.”

	Stear is coming off producing the critically-acclaimed dramas “Bruton,” which premiered at the 2026 Locarno Film Festival and recently won the Marquee Audience Award for Best Picture at the 2026 Austin Film Festival, as well as “Come With Me,” which premiered at the 2026 Beverly Hills Film Festival. Harvey was also an executive producer on the documentary “Dernsie: The Incredible Life of Bruce Dern” which premiered as an official selection of the 2026 Cannes Film Festival, as well as the 2026 Sitges Film Festival where it won best documentary, the 2026 SCAD Savannah Film Festival and the 2026 Beyond Fest.
	

	“I have long admired Emile’s work,” said Stear. “He is a remarkably creative artist who brings immense imagination to his characters, making him the perfect fit for the role of Will Tolbert in The Violet Crown. We are truly fortunate to have him as the lead of our film.”

	Bryan and Hirsch previously worked together on Sean Penn’s “Into The Wild.” 

	“I first met Emile 20 years ago in the snow capped mountains of Alaska and I instantly saw his uniqueness and the extraordinary talent that he brings to each role. He’s at the top of his game right now and I couldn’t be more thrilled to go on another adventure together,” said Bryan.

	Executive Producers include Ron Brooker and Anand Achanti.

	Since starring in Catherine Hardwicke’s “Lords of Dogtown,” Hirsch has worked with directors such as Nick Cassavetes (“Alpha Dog”), Sean Penn (“Into The Wild”), The Wachowskis (“Speed Racer”), William Friedkin (“Killer Joe”) and Quentin Tarantino (“Once Upon A Time In Hollywood”). He’s repped by UTA and Stride Management.

schema.headline: Emile Hirsch to Star in Texas-Set Thriller ‘The Violet Crown’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Blackpink’s Jisoo Gets Early Release Window on Tencent Music as Revenue Rises 5.6% to $1.3 Billion
description: China’s Tencent Music Entertainment Group secured 30-day early release windows for selected major K-pop titles, including Blackpink star Jisoo‘s la
body:
China’s Tencent Music Entertainment Group secured 30-day early release windows for selected major K-pop titles, including Blackpink star Jisoo‘s latest single, after renewing its deal with Hybe, as the company posted third-quarter revenue of RMB8.94 billion ($1.33 billion), up 5.6% year on year.

	The growth came as podcast and audiobook platform Ximalaya, whose acquisition TME completed in May, and rising concert and merchandise sales made up for a 15.7% decline in its social entertainment business.
	

	Music-related services, the company’s core segment, brought in RMB7.68 billion ($1.15 billion), a 10.2% rise. Membership revenue grew 9.2% to RMB4.99 billion ($744 million), with the premium SVIP tier adding both paying users and revenue per paying user. Marketing and consumption services, which cover advertising, live shows and artist merchandise, climbed 12.1% to RMB2.70 billion ($402 million). The company credited much of the merchandise and live growth to its work with Silence Wang, one of its strategic artists.

	Social entertainment and other revenue came to RMB1.26 billion ($188 million), down from RMB1.49 billion a year earlier. The changing mix trimmed gross margin to 42.8% from 43.5%.

	Net profit attributable to shareholders came in at RMB2.15 billion ($321 million), flat on the prior-year quarter, with diluted earnings of RMB1.36 ($0.20) per American depositary share (ADS) against RMB1.38. On a non-IFRS basis, attributable net profit edged up to RMB2.45 billion ($365 million) from RMB2.41 billion, and adjusted EBITDA grew 2.7% to RMB3.02 billion ($450 million). Operating expenses jumped 16.9% to RMB1.53 billion ($229 million), mostly due to the Ximalaya consolidation and the amortization of intangible assets tied to the acquisition.
	

	“Anchored in music, we are bringing IP to life across music, audio, live entertainment, and beyond. Ximalaya further enriches these experiences and creates more ways for users to engage,” said Cussion Pang, executive chair of TME.

	TME also renewed its partnership with YH Entertainment Group to shore up its Mandopop catalog, a move that sets up future merchandise tie-ins. It produced soundtracks for Tencent Video dramas, adding OSTs from series including “Against the Current” and “The Early Spring,” and worked with studios on several audiobook versions of “The Grave Robbers’ Chronicles.”

	Live events also expanded beyond China. TME put on four stadium shows for rapper Zhou Yan, known as GAI, drawing more than 120,000 fans, and hosted concerts for Will Pan, Shan Yichun, Steven Zhang and K-pop group Treasure. It backed Tia Ray’s first world tour, which took in Australia, Canada, Malaysia and the U.S., along with a performance at the Grammy Museum. JJ Lin, Lil Ghost and Tia Ray played the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix with the company’s support, and TME was a co-producer of the 2026 Pepsi Music Festival, whose lineup included Mayday’s Ashin and Jackson Wang.

	Fan engagement drove other campaigns. TME marked Bigbang’s 20th anniversary with online promotions and exhibitions in dozens of cities across mainland China, and brought Blackpink’s Jennie and i-dle’s Yuqi, among others, onto Weixin Video Accounts. Ximalaya added more than 10,000 motion comics aimed at short-session viewing.

	“Growing demand for richer pan-IP experiences, now complemented by Ximalaya’s offerings, is driving higher spending among both SVIP and other paying members, and we see further opportunity to capture a greater share of wallet,” said Ross Liang, TME’s CEO.

	The company ended September with RMB51.49 billion ($7.68 billion) in cash and short-term investments, up from RMB44.22 billion at the end of June. In September it sold $1 billion in senior unsecured notes, split evenly between tranches due 2031 and 2036. Over the quarter, TME bought back 34.7 million ADSs for roughly $300 million, at an average of $8.6 each.

	Listed in New York and Hong Kong, TME runs QQ Music, Kugou Music, Kuwo Music, WeSing and Ximalaya. Its third quarter showed the business moving further from social entertainment and toward stadiums, merch tables and audiobooks.

schema.headline: Blackpink’s Jisoo Gets Early Release Window on Tencent Music as Revenue Rises 5.6% to $1.3 Billion

title: Disney Quarterly Revenue Rises 16% and Profit Doubles; Company Forecasts $3 Billion in Annual Cost Savings by 2029 Including Through Layoffs
description: Disney had a robust quarter, topping Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines. But CEO Josh D’Amaro, who’s been in the job for eight mo
body:
Disney had a robust quarter, topping Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines. But CEO Josh D’Amaro, who’s been in the job for eight months, sees an opportunity for the company to become even more efficient and help fuel future growth.

	For the three months ended Oct. 3, 2026, which is Disney’s fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, the Mouse House reported revenue of $25.95 billion, up 16%, and a doubling of net income to $2.61 billion. Total operating segment income rose 43%, to $4.97 billion. The company reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.77. On average, Wall Street analysts expected revenue of $25.16 billion and adjusted earnings of $1.68 per share, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence.
	

	Overall, it was a solid quarter across Disney’s entertainment, sports and theme parks businesses. But D’Amaro and his lieutenants are looking to make Disney leaner and meaner. In their letter to shareholders accompanying the results, D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston provided an update to their “efficiency program to create incremental capacity to drive growth,” an initiative that has encompassed several rounds of job cutbacks in 2026.

	“We now expect the program to realize annual run-rate operating expense savings of about $3 billion by fiscal 2029,” the execs wrote. “While these efficiencies will be used primarily to fund future growth, we do expect a portion to drop to the bottom line over time.” Disney is poised to make a significant round of layoffs in the current quarter, affecting thousands of employees, with some managers reportedly told to cut expenses by 20% on an annualized basis.
	

	In addition, the execs said, they expect cash content spending in fiscal 2027 of approximately $26 billion, up about 9% from fiscal 2026. That includes “our increased investment in international programming and sports rights, and the timing of feature film production spend,” D’Amaro and Johnston said.

	Disney noted that its fourth quarter and fiscal 2026 results had one additional week of operations (a 53rd week) compared with the year-earlier period. The company estimates that the 53rd week contributed approximately 17 cents to full-year adjusted earnings per share.

	Revenue from Disney+ and Hulu rose 22% to $5.13 billion in the September 2026 quarter, and operating income more than doubled to $824 million. Disney said it expects to complete the integration of Disney+ and Hulu before the end of 2026, with a “fully unified experience” available in December.

	Starting with the December 2026 quarter, Disney will stop reporting operating income for Disney+ and Hulu. “We have made strong progress scaling our SVOD businesses and, as a result, see a long runway for growth and margin expansion at Disney Entertainment,” D’Amaro and Johnston wrote in the letter. “We no longer believe the supplemental disclosure of SVOD operating income reflects this segment focus and strategy.”

	In another financial reporting change, Disney as of Q1 of fiscal 2027 will provide additional revenue disclosures for Disney Entertainment, to “provide greater visibility into how we monetize Entertainment content across distribution platforms, third-party licensing and consumer products,” the company’s execs said.

	In the September quarter, Disney’s Entertainment segment overall saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income in the segment shot up 92% to $1.33 billion “due to growth in subscription and affiliate fees and higher content sales, partially offset by increased programming and production costs.”

	The execs touted the company’s intellectual-property flywheel between theatrical and streaming movie releases. Disney-Pixar’s “Toy Story 5,” which raked in $1.15 billion globally at the box office this summer, premiered on Disney+ on Sept. 23, and garnered 20 million views in its first five days on the platform. According to Disney, August was the highest month ever for Marvel Studios viewing, fueled by the summer theatrical success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” (released by Sony Pictures) and the debut of the “Avengers: Doomsday trailer.” During the quarter, Marvel content viewership on Disney+ more than doubled compared with its historical baseline. “Our successful rerelease of ‘Avengers: Endgame’ in late September also showed how anticipation continues to build for ‘Avengers: Doomsday,’ which arrives in theaters December 18,” D’Amaro and Johnston said in the letter.
	

	At ESPN, revenue increased 16% to $4.61 billion. Growth in subscription and affiliate fees came from an increase of 8% from the additional week of operations in the quarter compared with the year-earlier period, 6% from higher rates and 4% from Disney’s deal with the NFL giving the league a 10% ownership stake in ESPN.

	Disney Experiences revenue hit $10.11 billion in the September quarter, up 15%, with 5% of the growth in theme park admissions sales coming from higher average per capita ticket revenue. Segment operating income increased 20% to $2.25 billion. Disney Experiences saw an 11% increase in global visitors in the quarter (or a 4% increase excluding the 53rd week). “We continued to see headwinds from lower international attendance at our domestic parks in the quarter, but as expected, those headwinds moderated from the year-over-year impact observed in the third quarter,” D’Amaro and Johnston said.

	For fiscal 2027, Disney is expecting double-digit growth in adjusted EPS (excluding the impact of the 53rd week in ’26). The company forecast total segment operating income growth of approximately 8%, factoring in the exclusion of equity income reporting from entertainment segment operating results. Disney expects the majority of its growth in total segment operating income and adjusted EPS for fiscal 2027 to occur in the first half of the fiscal year.

	In fiscal ’27, Disney expects capital expenditures of approximately $9 billion “as we continue to execute against our strategy to turbocharge growth at Disney Experiences,” the execs said. The company invested $8.7 billion parks, resorts and other property in the 2026 fiscal year.

	In August, Disney closed the sale of its 50% stake in A+E Global Media to co-owner Hearst for $1.2 billion in cash. For fiscal 2026, A+E contributed approximately $390 million in equity income to Disney’s Entertainment segment operating income. 

	Also Tuesday, Disney’s board declared a cash dividend of $2.00 per share payable over the course of fiscal 2027, a 33% increase over the $1.50 per share paid to shareholders during fiscal year 2026.

schema.headline: Disney Quarterly Revenue Rises 16% and Profit Doubles; Company Forecasts $3 Billion in Annual Cost Savings by 2029 Including Through Layoffs

title: Ali Fazal, Fiona Shaw, Naseeruddin Shah, Tom Mison Lead Richie Mehta’s ‘A Passage to India’ Series for BBC, CBC
description: Ali Fazal (“Mirzapur”), Tom Mison and Fiona Shaw are leading the cast of “A Passage to India,” Emmy-winning “Delhi Crime” filmmaker Richie Mehta’s
body:
Ali Fazal (“Mirzapur”), Tom Mison and Fiona Shaw are leading the cast of “A Passage to India,” Emmy-winning “Delhi Crime” filmmaker Richie Mehta’s five-part series version of E.M. Forster’s classic novel for the BBC and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

	Mehta wrote the adaptation and is now directing it on location in India.

	Set in the 1920s, the drama follows Aziz (Fazal), a local doctor who has spent years caring for others and who sets out to convince his Indian friends that real friendship with the British can survive colonial rule. His hopes start to come apart after an unexplained episode at the Marabar caves, which leaves him accused of assault.
	

	The scandal stirs up violent feeling and builds to a trial that grips the public. As the case plays out, the lives of everyone involved are upended, and Aziz and those closest to him begin to grasp how deeply colonization has shaped them.

	Mison (“De Gaulle: Resistance,” “See”) plays Fielding, an elusive teacher who becomes close to Aziz. BAFTA winner Shaw (“Bad Sisters,” “Killing Eve”) is Mrs. Moore, a woman who has led a varied life and who comes to India to see her son Ronny (Gwilym Lee, “The Great,” “Bohemian Rhapsody”) and set up a match between him and Adela (Clare Hughes, “Ponies,” “Ten Pound Poms”).

	Naseeruddin Shah (“Paar,” “The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen”) plays Godbole, who teaches alongside Fielding at his college and offers spiritual grounding as the crisis deepens. Shahana Goswami (“Santosh,” “Four Years Later”) is Amrit Rao, Aziz’s barrister, who has just become India’s first woman lawyer. Danish Hussain (“Haq,” “Tanaav”) plays Hamidullah, Aziz’s uncle and closest friend, who doubts the cross-cultural bonds Aziz believes in.
	

	“Adapting ‘A Passage to India’ has been a dream of mine for as long as I’ve been telling stories,” Mehta said. “To reinterpret the complex and intriguing characters that E.M. Forster masterfully conjured from his experiences over a century ago, and finding in them a relevance that resonates so deeply with today’s world, has been a real joy, and I believe it makes for incredibly gripping drama.”

	Parti Productions (“The Boy with the Topknot”), Working Title Television (“Jo Nesbø’s Detective Hole”) and Mehta’s A Passage Post, a subsidiary of his Poor Man’s Productions (“Poacher”), are producing the show. The BBC and CBC commissioned it for BBC One, BBC iPlayer, CBC TV and CBC Gem, and it qualifies as an official U.K.-Canada co-production. Working Title Television sits within Universal Studio Group’s Universal Global Television division. NBCUniversal Global TV Distribution is handling worldwide sales.

	Nisha Parti, founder of Parti Productions and an executive producer on the show, said she was honored to be bringing the story to television after almost 10 years of working with Mehta. “To tell the story of British colonial rule, which shaped all our families, from an Indian perspective feels like a first. This beautiful novel tackles that and so much more,” she said. “We’ve seen many romanticized versions of India on screen over the years, so I’m so grateful to Working Title Television and Universal Global Television for understanding why our version needs to be told now and helping bring it to life, and to the BBC and CBC for being such brilliant partners.”

	Mehta and Parti serve as executive producers along with Working Title Television’s Surian Fletcher-Jones, Eric Fellner and Tim Bevan, the BBC’s Nawfal Faizullah, CBC’s Nicola Makoway and Roma Khanna. Kristian Dench is series producer.

	“‘A Passage to India’ is one of the great stories about friendship, and how quickly suspicion and power can tear it apart,” said Fletcher-Jones, who is head of drama at Working Title Television. “Richie has understood that from the very start, and his scripts handle it with real care and honesty.”

	Lindsay Salt, director of BBC Drama, said Mehta’s pitch had blown the broadcaster away. “He has crafted a version of extraordinary depth and sensitivity, and we’re thrilled to be working with him and our partners at Parti Productions, Working Title Television, A Passage Post and CBC,” she said.
	

	Forster’s 1924 novel has been adapted before. Santha Rama Rau turned it into a stage play in 1960, and Waris Hussein directed a version of that play for BBC One’s “Play of the Month” strand in 1965. David Lean’s 1984 feature, also drawn from Rau’s play, earned 11 Oscar nominations and won two, including best supporting actress for Peggy Ashcroft as Mrs. Moore.

	CBC plans to bring the series to viewers in Canada, the U.K. and beyond, working with the BBC and NBCUniversal. Each of the five episodes runs 60 minutes.

schema.headline: Ali Fazal, Fiona Shaw, Naseeruddin Shah, Tom Mison Lead Richie Mehta’s ‘A Passage to India’ Series for BBC, CBC

title: Christopher Hampton on AI – ‘I’m More Interested in Real Intelligence’– and Dos and Don’t’s of Screenwriting
description: “The least they could do,” Sir Christopher Hampton said about Glenn Close’s Honorary Oscar at the Tallinn Film Festival where at a masterclass, “Fr
body:
“The least they could do,” Sir Christopher Hampton said about Glenn Close’s Honorary Oscar at the Tallinn Film Festival where at a masterclass, “From Stage to Screen, The Art of Adaptation,” the two-time Oscar winner delivered sometimes trenchant takes on AI – ‘I’m more interested in real intelligence’ – and how screenwriting was like gambling at a casino.

	“It’s about time!,” Hampton said of Close’s Honorary Oscar.“I was very happy to hear that. I think she’s still hoping to get one for acting in a specific role, but that hasn’t happened yet, so the least they could do was giving her an Honorary Oscar, I guess”
	

	Unpacking a list of dos and don’ts for screenwriting, using AI was definitely not on the to-do side. In fact, he couldn’t care less about the topic.

	Comparing AI to “a sort of super Google,” Hampton said “AI hasn’t troubled me very much. I’m more interested in real intelligence, and I think the flaw in artificial intelligence is in the name because it’s artificial.”

	Asked whether he thought AI could replace screenwriters he said: “I don’t think it’s gonna happen, as ‘our ‘work is more interesting than ‘its’ work.” And for those newcomers tempted by writing a script with the help of AI he said: “You’re being lazy by allowing some other some other external force to take over you; you might as well choose a different profession.”

	In fact, at the opening session of the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event’s training program Discovery Campus, Hampton who is also juror at the festival’s official selection, warned newcomers about the hardships of screenwriting and of works actually landing on screens.
	

	“Writing for film is really like going into the casino, he said. “You sit at the table, you put your money under 20 and the chances of the film being made the way you imagined are so tiny that when it does happen, it’s incredibly, incredibly fulfilling and it gives you an enormous amount of pleasure. But most of the time, the croupier just takes the chips away and that’s it!!”

	Scripts Waiting in the Drawers

	He said aspiring scribes should accept the fact that “there’s a lot of wastage in writing. A lot of projects that you will spend six, nine months or a year writing, will never be seen in any form because somehow, they haven’t been financed.”

	Numerous of his works have never been filmed, he admitted, despite his stellar career as playwright, screenwriter, translator and director spanning five decades that earned him multiple nods and a knighthood for services to drama,

	Hampton mentioned an adaptation of the life of Dmitri Shostakovich, “his struggles as a composer in the Soviet Union,” written three-four years ago. “I haven’t been able to get it made because people don’t want to engage with or don’t want to make a film about Russia, set in Russia, dealing with Russians. I find it paradoxical because of course it’s just the time when it would be interesting to see a film about a man who struggled his whole life with the political system and somehow found ways to circumvent all the roadblocks that were put in his way,” he added.

	Similarly, another project set in Indonesia in the 1950s, against the background of a conflict between fundamentalist and moderate Muslims, was rejected by financiers due to the topic viewed as problematic at the time, just post 09/11.

	He also underscored that many of his works have taken years – sometimes decades – to turn into features. “My projects are very, very slow,” he acknowledged, citing David Cronenberg’s “A Dangerous Method” that took 14 years, and his directorial debut “Carrington” (a double winner at Cannes 1995) 18 years from script to screen. As for the anticipated “Embers” starring Ralph Fiennes and Viggo Mortensen, Hampton said the screen adaptation of Sándor Márais’s acclaimed novel, lined up for 2027, has been 20 years in the making. “I finally got it made with the director I wanted, the great Hungarian director István Szabó,” he said.
	

	“You just have to be patient!” advised Hampton who still hopes that some films that have been waiting 30-40 years might still be picked up, such as the David Lean adaptation of Joseph Conrad’s 1904 novel “Nostromo,” which was shelved partly due to the director’s failing health and eventual death in 1991.

	Screenwriting Tips

	Unpacking the art of screenwriting, Hampton said Lean, the Oscar-winning British director of “Lawrence of Arabia “was together with the legendary Fred Zinneman (“High Noon,” “From Here to Eternity”) two filmmakers who had determining influences on him.

	Having started in 1973 with the adaptation of Ibsen’s “A Doll’s House,” starring Anthony Hopkins, he said it took him more than a decade to fully grasp the difference between writing for theatre – something that came easily to him – and writing for film.“I didn’t realise that moving from a stage play to a film was more than simply repeating the dialogue in front of a camera. And it took me about 10 years to figure out how not to make a film from a play which smelt like the theatre.”

	The mistake he made was thinking that it was easier to write films than theatre plays, he reckoned. “In other words, you think a film gives you enormous liberty, you can jump from London to Hong Kong in one cut, but that liberty imposes on you a number of constraints that I hadn’t been aware of before,” he said.

	From working with Lean, he learned “how to make a scene flow into another, even if it’s in a different location or a different subject,” and he learned to respect “a film’s cohesion, although it might be cut into several chapters like a novel.

	From working nine months with Fred Zinnemann (“High Noon,” From Here to Eternity”) on a project about the last days of WWII – eventually cancelled following a change of boss at 20th Century Fox, he learned to focus on “telling the story, just the story.”

	After his collaboration with Lean and Zinnemann, Hampton said he went straight to working on Stephen Frears’ “Dangerous Liaisons.” “For the first time after 10-15 years of writing screenplays, I felt like I kind of knew what I was doing.”

	Cronenberg was another visionary filmmaker who had an impact on him and from whom he picked up how to be “more economical,” something he then applied for instance while writing the first draft of Florian Zeller’s “The Son (2022). “The first thing I did was cut 20 pages!” said the screenwriter who insisted on keeping a story to its core.
	

	“One of the most important skills that you can achieve as a screenwriter is to know what you need to say and don’t say any more than that. It’s really a question of defining what’s essential,” he noted.

	Expanding on the subject, he said that some filmmakers unnecessarily, feel the urge to over-explain, underestimating the audience “who is always more intelligent than people imagine.” He said U.S. Studios with their numerous notes, often ask him “to explain this or that,” things that “are there in the script already that they haven’t noticed.”

	Hampton went on criticising Hollywood’s formula filmmaking, blockbusters based on universes, that “actually I find completely incomprehensible,” he admitted.He also pointed at the U.S. studios’ aversion for ‘original’ works. He said during a test-screening of his 2003 “Imagining Argentina,” one of three works he directed, when a young member of the audience described the film as being original “the [studio] executive next to me put his face in his hands and groaned because there’s nothing more difficult for them than something that’s original.”

	Similarly, Hampton dismissed today’s TV drama, after being asked by Variety if he was tempted by the format. Unlike in the 1970s, when he would write “a lot” for the BBC when they would produce two to three TV plays and films a week, he said he wasn’t tempted by what he calls “a brutal medium” today. The last series he worked on was “The Singapore Grip” which aired on ITV in 2020.

	“It took me such a long time, and there were so many notes to negotiate from the people making it. I just thought television really wasn’t worth it anymore,” he said.While acknowledging that television “provides an enormous amount of work for writers” today, he described the form as probably “the most constricted, prescriptive and unimaginative.” “I don’t really understand why the freedom that we used to have when I was young – and was very lucky to have –~ no longer exists,” he stated.



	

					Christopher Hampton at his Tallinn masterclass

schema.headline: Christopher Hampton on AI – ‘I’m More Interested in Real Intelligence’– and Dos and Don’t’s of Screenwriting

title: Kid Rock's Nashville Bar Sued By Man Who Claims Security Guards Beat Him Up
description:
Kid Rock's Nashville Bar Sued
                          Security Guards Whooped My Butt!!!
body:
Kid Rock's Nashville Bar Sued
                          Security Guards Whooped My Butt!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 17, 2026
                            1:00 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kid Rock's honky tonk has been dealing with some legal drama all summer long ... because the controversial rock star's Nashville bar is being sued by a man who claims security guards went overboard and beat him senseless.
      
    
            A man named Joshua Welch is suing Kid Rock's Big Honky Tonk and Steakhouse over an alleged incident he says took place in December 2025 ... and the alleged beatdown kicked off after he says he "lightly tapped" a performer's guitar with his finger.
      
    
            Welch's lawyer says he touched the guitar in a "moment of poor judgment" -- and didn’t even touch the instrument hard ... but he claims he was still approached by a security guard and 86'd from the joint.
      

            On his way out of the venue, Welch's lawyer says he doubled down by trying to touch the guitar again ... which is when he claims the security guard became "disproportionately agitated."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Welch claims he was beaten by 3 men in the elevator. He alleges he was slammed against the wall of the elevator and then thrown out when it reached the ground floor. He says he was then pushed to the floor and repeatedly shoved down when he tried to get off the ground multiple times ... including once when he says he landed hard on his right hand and badly injured his ring finger.
      
    
            He says he underwent surgery to fix the damaged digit about a month later.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Welch is suing for assault and battery, negligence, negligent hiring and training, and false imprisonment. To be clear, he's suing Kid Rock's restaurant -- not the star himself.
      
    
            In its reply, the restaurant denied all wrongdoing ... and insisted its security guards were justified in their use of force.

Ray's death is under investigation, and his cause and manner of death are pending further study.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... Heidi is grieving the loss and is surrounded by family and friends during this difficult time.

            Ray shared photos showing the two of them together at the time ... including one where the pair locked lips and another in which she looked at him adoringly.
      
    
            Ray rose to prominence in the late 2000s as a short film and music video director. He was part of Court 13 -- the filmmaking collective that made the movie "Beasts of the Southern Wild."
      
    
            Ray's mom, renowned script supervisor and set photographer Mary Cybulski, passed away from Glioblastoma in November of 2025.
      
    
            Heidi was a cast member on "Saturday Night Live" from 2017 until she was cut after the 2025 season. She was previously married to 'Marvel' writer Zeb Wells.
      
    
            Ray was 43.
      
    
            RIP.

title: Ryan Lochte's Ex-Wife Kayla Reid Auctioning Off Wedding Ring for Fresh Start
description:
Ryan Lochte's Ex-Wife Kayla Reid
                          My Kids Come Before My Carats ...
body:
Ryan Lochte's Ex-Wife Kayla Reid
                          My Kids Come Before My Carats ...
                          Auctioning Wedding Ring
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                November 16, 2026
                
                            2:00 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 16, 2026
                                3:08 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Ryan Lochte's ex-wife is turning her old wedding ring into cold, hard cash ... hoping the massive diamond will help dig her out of debt following their messy divorce, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Kayla Rae Reid tells TMZ ... she's auctioning off the ring after being left with significant debt from her divorce ... saying she's raising their three children with very little financial support and carrying most of the financial burden herself.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            But Kayla insists she's not just trying to unload a painful reminder of her marriage ... telling us, "I see it more as taking something from my past and reinvesting it into my future."
      

            She says there's no point in having something so valuable collecting dust in a drawer when it could help her rebuild her life and provide a more secure future for her kids.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The ring is no small chunk of change ... featuring a 4.37-carat center diamond and 77 smaller diamonds, totaling 5.11 carats. Kayla recalls Ryan spending around $60,000 on it in 2016 ... though she's not certain of the price.
      
    
            She's now partnered with luxury jewelry auction platform Worthy to sell the ring ... hoping to pay off debt and potentially donate a portion of the proceeds to women rebuilding their lives after difficult marriages.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... the former couple finalized their divorce in July, with Kayla receiving primary custody of their children and Ryan agreeing to pay $1,000 a month in child support, with no alimony.
      
    
            For Kayla, it's less about parting with the past ... and more about cashing in on a fresh start.
